Apply the Darcy–Weisbach equation to calculate the major pressure drop along a horizontal straight pipe with no fittings or minor losses.
Use water at 20 °C as the working fluid with density ρ = 998 kg/m³ and dynamic viscosity μ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s.
Model the pipe as a smooth-ended circular duct with internal diameter D = 0.050 m, length L = 100 m, and wall absolute roughness ε = 0.15 mm (galvanized iron).
Establish the volumetric flow rate as Q = 2 L/s = 0.002 m³/s, which corresponds to an average velocity v = Q / A ≈ 1.02 m/s in the pipe cross-section A = π D²/4.
Compute the Reynolds number as Re = ρ v D / μ and verify that the flow regime is turbulent; classify it as laminar or turbulent accordingly before selecting the friction factor formula.
Determine the Darcy friction factor f using the Colebrook–White equation 1/√f = −2 log₁₀( ε/(3.7D) + 2.51/(Re√f) ), iterated to convergence, and validate the result against the Moody chart for relative roughness ε/D = 0.003.
Report the final result as the frictional pressure drop ΔP = f (L/D) (ρ v²/2) in Pa (and equivalently in bar or meters of water column head loss).
State all intermediate quantities (Re, ε/D, f) together with the final ΔP so the calculation can be independently reproduced.
Assume isothermal, steady-state, single-phase flow with no elevation change, no minor losses from bends, valves, or fittings, and no entrance/exit effects.
